What this comparison does—and doesn’t—prove

These are calculated meshes, not generated pictures. Both use the same neutral material and lighting so their shapes can be compared. The game's textures, shadows, distant rendering, and close-up blur are not reproduced here. Caching itself changes no pixels.

This checkout is behind the live site. The baseline is a saved code snapshot, not a capture of the latest production renderer. Newer main already has additional normal smoothing for loose ground, so this preview must not be read as its before/after.

The baseline runs src/world/surfaceMesh.js (). The experiment inserts relaxation before that same mesher triangulates and clips the surface. Each pass moves a point halfway toward its quad-edge neighbors' mean, then clamps it to its original dual grid cube. The input padding grows with the pass count. No edge-preservation rule is added. Triangle counts can change because previously collapsed faces open up and the moved surface intersects crop boundaries differently.

“Dig a crater” removes the same sphere of cells from both inputs, then rebuilds both complete specimens. It shows the resulting shape—not production edit scheduling, edit latency, or a seam between two different rendering methods.

Mesh bytes below count positions, normals, material IDs, and triangle indices only. They exclude input cells, scratch arrays, the viewer, and GPU copies. Building a smoother mesh costs extra work; drawing it is not automatically faster. No neural model runs here.
